text.en: When you were very small, your world might have been just your home. As you grew, it became bigger. This short anonymous poem is about a young bird who learns, step by step, that the world is much larger than it first seemed. Let us fly with it.

Think about where you see birds and what they do. Would you like to fly like a bird, and why? Also think about what a baby bird imagines about its world. The poem answers that question. Four useful words: pale means light in colour, lightly means gently, finally means at last, and labour means work.
The young bird says it first lived in a little house, and lived there very well. It thought the world was small and round and made of pale blue shell. This is the egg, so the bird remembers its first home. The world seemed small, round and blue because that was all the bird could see inside the egg.
Next the bird lived in a little nest and needed nothing more. It thought the world was made of straw because the nest was made of straw, and it nestled close to its mother. The word nestled shows that the baby bird was warm and comfortable.
One day the bird fluttered out of its nest to see what it could find. It said that the world was made of leaves, but then it admitted that it had been very blind. It could not tell the leaves from inside the nest, so it did not know about the wider world. The bird steps out into the world, and its first guess about the world is changed by what it sees.
At length the bird flew beyond the tree, quite fit for grown-up labours, which means it was now strong enough to do the work of an adult bird. It ends by saying it does not know how the world is made, and neither do its neighbours. The poem teaches that the world is bigger than we first think, and that learning never really ends. Even grown-ups do not know everything.
The stanzas go in order: the bird lives happily in a small world, lives in a cosy nest with its mother, steps out into the world, and flies away as an adult. The bird changed its house two times, from the shell to the nest. Describing words in the poem are pale, blue, round, straw and little. You can add pointed, small, green, wooden, thin, hanging, brown and round. The neighbours are probably other birds, since the poet says they do not know either.
In the poem, well rhymes with shell, and the book asks you to find more rhyming words for each stanza, such as fell and sell. Rhyming words end with the same sound. A poem uses them to make a pattern. Try finishing a stanza with rhyming ends: I fly high and I fly low, but one thing I surely know, whenever I wish to rest, my little nest is the best. Reading aloud with a steady rhythm helps you notice the rhyme.
To speak as a bird say which bird you are, what colour and size, where you live, what you do in the day and what message you have for humans. To write about how a baby or a fish might see the world, copy the style: first my world was, after that, in the end. In the exploration, list the materials your home is made of, such as bricks, cement, wood and glass, and think about why homes are not made of straw. Builders include the mason who lays bricks and stones, the painter, electrician, plumber, carpenter and architect, each with their own work.

problem.en: Match each stanza with its main idea: shell world, nest world, leaf world, flying beyond the tree.

text.en: Read the first line of each stanza and notice the home.

why.en: Each stanza names a different place.

text.en: Stanza 1: happy in a small world; stanza 2: cosy nest with mother; stanza 3: steps out into the world; stanza 4: flies as a grown-up bird.
Find a word with the same ending sound.

why.en: Rhyming words share the last sound.

text.en: Shell is in the poem, and fell, bell and sell are also rhymes.

why.en: They all end with the same sound.

prompt.en: Explain how the bird's idea of the world changed in the poem and why.

requiredIdeas.en: At first the world was a small round blue shell.
Then it was a nest of straw with its mother.
Then it was leaves when the bird fluttered out.
Finally the bird flew beyond the tree and realised nobody knows how the world is made.

commonMisconceptions.en: The bird never left its nest.
The bird was sure about everything.

points.en: What a Bird Thought is a four-stanza anonymous poem.
The bird thinks the world is a shell, then a straw nest, then leaves, then something bigger.
The word blind means it did not see the wider world.
The poem shows that we keep learning as our world grows.
Rhyming words end with the same sound, such as well and shell.
